title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The failure here is at the data-collection stage of model training. Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack indicates the sources included YouTube, Deezer, and Genius. No licensing agreements with rights holders were in place before training began. The system was then deployed publicly and used to generate music that, when prompted with genre, era, and stylistic cues, produced outputs closely resembling specific copyrighted recordings.

This is a case of a system built on unlicensed source material being deployed at commercial scale. The failure would have required catching before training, not after: the decision about what data to include in a training corpus is made once, and a model that has already ingested infringing material cannot be retroactively corrected by changes to the product interface. The outputs themselves, near-identical recreations of identifiable songs, are a downstream symptom of a decision made at the data-curation stage.

What is not established is intent to infringe. The lawsuits are allegations, a German court ruled against Suno on GEMA's claims, some cases settled, and others remain active, but no final adjudication on all claims has been reported. The class actions from independent artists and the suits from publishers such as Round Hill are ongoing proceedings, not verdicts.

summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and others, have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse these companies of illegally copying thousands of copyrighted songs to train their AI models without permission or payment. The lawsuits claim that Udio and Suno have been deliberately secretive about their training data and that their business model fundamentally relies on copyright infringement at a massive scale. The record labels submitted a huge list documenting thousands of scraped works from famous artists like The Beatles, Michael Jackson, Coldplay, and many others.

To build their case, the record labels tested both AI generators using specific prompts describing songs by era, genre, and artist characteristics. They claim to have successfully recreated versions of famous songs, including near-identical copies of tracks like Green Day's "American Idiot" and Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." One example involved generating 29 different outputs mimicking Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode." The lawsuits, filed in New York and Massachusetts, set up a major legal battle over how generative AI services can use copyrighted material during training.
